  • Source: _ingest/raw/ice/articles.jsonl (783 full-text items, 2018-03 → 2026-10-22). Read in full for this note: every leadership/board release (Vice retirement 2020-01-21; Hill → Gardiner 2021-03-02; the 2021-12-06 senior-leadership release with Sprecher's staff letter; futures leaders 2022-06-29; Edmonds/King 2023-10-26; board elections 2020-08, 2020-12, 2022-03, Lord Hill 2025-09-18; Bakkt CEO changes 2019–20; Serafini, Klima, Rowe, Tuttle/Blaugrund); the seven shareholder letters (2019–2025); and the podcast transcripts where ICE leaders speak at length — Sprecher 2018-04-03, 2019-11-27 (posted 2020-02-12), 2020-05-08, 2024-08-12; Jackson 2018-10-25; Martin 2022-03-08; Tyrrell 2022-03-21; Edmonds 2022-06-27 and 2026-01-14; Wassersug 2023-01-03; Bowler 2024-11-04; Grey/Pawar 2025-05-12; Blaugrund/Herrick 2026-02-18; Bowen 2022-02-14. Attributed quotes were pulled by script for ~30 executives and dated from release text. Caveats: (1) all company-published; podcasts are hosted by ICE's own communications chief; (2) no earnings-call transcripts or proxy statements, so pay, tenure detail and succession planning are invisible; (3) the undated WatersTechnology profile of Edmonds is dated "April 2024" (in-text).
  • Core claim: ICE is the opposite of Tradeweb's choreographed handover. One founder has been Chair and CEO for 26 years and wrote in Dec 2021, “I’m not going anywhere, but for many years, we’ve been working to develop the next generation of ICE leaders” — and no successor is named anywhere in the corpus through Oct 2026. Development happens by rotation, not by heir-designation: a CDS-clearing builder (Edmonds) runs Fixed Income & Data; the LIBOR administrator (Bowler) runs mortgage technology; the IR head (Gardiner) becomes CFO; the NYSE COO (Blaugrund) becomes the tokenization lead; the FIDS president (Martin) runs the NYSE. Ben Jackson stays President throughout, so the obvious No. 2 is a fixture rather than an heir. The connective tissue is a founder's script that every level repeats — "analog to digital," "all-weather," "connect people to opportunity," "neutral" — which is how a centralized, founder-led firm keeps a 10,000-person, five-segment company sounding like one company. Where leaders differ, it is on timing and politics (crypto, ESG, cloud, Texas), not on the playbook.

Board of directors: 14 after Cooper and Mulhern joined (2020-12-07: “increase the ICE Board of Directors to 14 members, including five women and nine men”) → 13 after Jean-Marc Forneri's death (2020-12-28) → 10 after the May 2022 meeting, when three pre-IPO directors left (Crisp, Salerno, Tese; Salerno had been Lead Independent Director since 2008, succeeded by Thomas Noonan), leaving the board to “stand at 10 members, including six women and four men” (2022-03-04) → 11 with Lord Hill (2025-09-18: “expands from 10 to 11 directors”).

What the chart says. - No heir, by design (inference). Every top seat except CFO and COO changed hands in 2019–26; the CEO and President seats did not. The Dec 2021 reshuffle is said to “draw entirely from deep and diverse talent within the organization” (release text) and is framed as "good governance," not succession. - Rotation is the development system. Edmonds: clearing → sales → CDO (with marketing) → FIDS. Bowler: IBA → clearing → mortgage. de Ruig: futures COO → IBA. Martin: FIDS → NYSE (still FIDS Chair). Blaugrund: NYSE COO → ICE strategic initiatives. Bland: one exchange → all exchanges. Bland's own line: “ICE has always benefitted from creating and cultivating a deep bench of talent across our global operations” (2022-06-29). - Gravity pulls to Atlanta. Edmonds moved from Chicago because the FIDS president should “sit in Atlanta with the rest of senior leadership” (profile, Apr 2024, in-text); Hindlian left because Hindlian “has elected to remain rooted in the New York area” (2023-10-26). Location is a selection criterion. - Outside hires come in for regulation, not for running a segment: Klima (CFTC), Serafini (JPM/Goldman risk), Bowen and Lord Hill (board). The acquired-company heads (Tyrrell from Ellie Mae; Black Knight's Grey and Walden) stay a level down or move on. - Subsidiary boards feed the parent board. Silver also joined ICE Clear Europe's board; Mulhern sat on Ellie Mae's; Tirinnanzi came from the IMT and MERS boards; Lord Hill from ICE Endex. Directors are pre-vetted inside the group.

2. Profiles

Jeffrey Sprecher — founder (2000), Chair & CEO

Background: bought a failing Atlanta power-trading firm (Continental Power Exchange); not from Wall Street: “I suspect I'm the only chairman of the New York Stock Exchange that never has traded, never has worked at a bank” (2018-04-03). Talks about: the playbook, deal discipline, neutrality, crises as launch windows, culture as productive conflict. - Deal doctrine. “I've never been the low bidder.” Customers as owners: “I gave away, actually, 80% of the equity to the customers in exchange for a commitment that they would try it and use it.” (both 2018-04-03). - Neutral operator. “for an exchange operator, you're neutral party. You're Switzerland.” And patience: “The market really will resist the revolution.” (Abu Dhabi, 2019-11-27). - Identity. “I would probably call it the Intercontinental Massively Scalable Network and Database Company because that's what we are.” “In my mind I really am not a public company CEO, I'm a small business entrepreneur” (both 2020-05-08). - Crises as windows. Defending the mortgage bets into the rate trough: “it's easier to start a new initiative and have market acceptance of your initiative during periods of stress.” Treasury clearing as Geithner's barn redux: “An even bigger barn.” (Sprecher repeating King, 2024-08-12). - Culture. “That's a culture that I guess the tone starts at the top with me to a certain degree, but it's the only tone I know” (2024-08-12). Sprecher credits an organizational-behavior class: good companies have internal conflict and good conflict resolution. - Succession and the bench. The only document is the 2021 letter: “it’s more important than ever to challenge our leaders to take on new tasks and acquire new skills” and “Challenging this group of global leaders with new or expanded roles is fundamental to good governance and stewardship of our firm.” Sprecher gave up the NYSE chair with the self-description “the least qualified person to ever have that title in a 200+ year history” (2024-08-12). - Optimistic about millennial homebuying, Treasury clearing, AI, prediction markets. Self-deprecating about the brand: people “don't know whether it's ice cubes or whether it's the immigration service or whatever” (2024-08-12).

Ben Jackson — President (throughout)

Talks about: fixed income data-first, M&A integration, culture imprinting. The 2018 podcast is the corpus's most explicit FI strategy: “many, many different service providers have tried to start with just building an execution platform and have failed.” Jackson names the RFQ incumbents once — “those being MarketAxess Bloomberg and Tradeweb ... tend to be RFQ-driven.” — and concedes “In fixed income, it's early days.” (2018-10-25). On acquisitions: “we've prided ourselves on putting our imprint on each individual company that we acquire” and acquired firms run as “its own little fiefdom” until ICE flattens them. Later voice is operational: “Margins have been compressed to historic lows” (mortgage lenders, 2024-05-15); “The systems we run are the backbone of global financial markets.” (2026-06-03, Anthropic Project Glasswing). Read: Jackson owns deals end-to-end (17 items in corpus) yet never speaks about succession or the President's own role. Eight years after "early days," ICE bought MarketAxess (ice marketaxess deal).

Lynn Martin — FIDS President → NYSE Group President (2022–), FIDS Chair

Talks about: data as input and output, humans plus machines, the floor, listings politics. The most-mentioned executive after Sprecher (63 items). “data is the most important output of fully-transparent liquid markets, but then it's a really important input to finding fair value.” Pricing 2.8M bonds: “we also do it with 200 humans.” Candid about growth: “what got us the growth rates we had for the last six and a half years is not what's going to drive our growth” (all 2022-03-08). - Shift (the sharpest at ICE). 2022: “ESG is a primary focus of the leaders I speak with” (2022-03-09). 2025: NYSE Texas opens with Trump Media as first listing — “We are thrilled to open NYSE Texas to corporate issuers and to welcome Trump Media & Technology Group to our NYSE community” (2025-03-31); credit to “the pro-business environment fostered by Governor Abbott in the Lone Star State” (2025-12-01). 2026, in the Trump–Xi delegation: “President Trump has made American AI leadership an explicit national priority.” But the same speech insists “women need seats at the table before the frameworks are finalized” (2026-05-15) — a pro-administration frame with the 2022 inclusion agenda kept inside it.

Chris Edmonds — CDS clearing builder → Clearing & Risk → CDO → FIDS President (2024–)

Background: OTC gas broker at ICAP from 1997, "competitors" with Sprecher; joined 2010 to run ICE Clear Credit; Alabama-born, Chicago-based 13 years. Sprecher calls Edmonds “distinguished as one of ICE’s most skillful operators” (2023-10-26). Talks about: clearing discipline, regulatory catalysts, data in the AI era, the client relationship. - Clearing philosophy (2022-06-27, vs FTX). “What we're doing is refereeing not the value, but the performance.” The brief from the founder: “Jeff, I heard don't let the clearing houses blow up and make sure everyone understands our message.” Humility as house style: “We don't know everything. We're not the smartest people in the room”. - Speaks the script. “this company is about transitioning from analog to digital.” (2022); “You’ve heard our CEO talk about the analog to digital transformation” (Apr 2024); “indispensable in connecting people to opportunity” (2023-10-26). - Identity claim. “We’re not an exchange group or a venue that is needing to buy technology—we create technology” (Apr 2024) — written two years before ICE bought MarketAxess's technology. - Broker's relationship ethic. “I need to know their kids’ names.” (Apr 2024). - Candour (2026-01-14). Disputes the interviewer's e-trading share: “I might challenge you on that statistic.” Admits the mandate drove entry: “I don't believe without the regulatory catalyst that we would have made the decision to enter that.” On the mortgage roll-up: “Not sure that everyone understood why or when we were doing it. Jeff had a great vision of what that would look like.” Shift: in 2024 Treasury clearing was “maybe a worst kept secret.” (clip); in 2026 it is mandate-dependent.

Warren Gardiner (CFO 2021–) and Scott Hill (CFO 2007–21)

Sprecher praised Hill as “a visionary for our growth, steward of our culture, and mentor to many” (2021-03-02) — Hill also ran HR and IR, and at times clearing. Gardiner's credential is communication: led IR "since 2017," ex-sell-side analyst, and “his intimate knowledge of our industry, business, and culture has positioned him well” (Sprecher, 2021-03-02). Gardiner is the second voice in every quarterly earnings release from 2Q21 ("Warren Gardiner, ICE Chief Financial Officer, added:") and speaks at each deal: Black Knight “will further complement our 'all weather' business model” (2022-05-04) and MarketAxess “exemplifies the discipline and long-term perspective that define how ICE approaches capital allocation” (2026-07-30). Inference: ICE chose a CFO who already knew what the market wanted to hear; the IR seat is a pipeline (Loeffler: IR/marketing → Bakkt CEO; Gardiner: IR → CFO).

Stuart Williams (COO 2022–) — the silent operator

Moved from running ICE Futures Europe; reports to Jackson. One attributed quote in the whole corpus (EU allowances to the Netherlands, 2021-02-08). Wassersug explains the swap: Williams “was looking for another opportunity himself. So it was a perfect opportunity to put Stuart in” (2023-01-03). Read: the COO job is internal plumbing, not a public succession signal.

Stacey Cunningham (NYSE President 2018–21)

Spoke for the NYSE through COVID: “NYSE’s trading floors provide unique value to issuers and investors, but our markets are fully capable of operating in an all-electronic fashion” (2020-03-18). Sprecher's farewell credits a tech overhaul, direct listings and ESG: “Stacey embraced the challenge as ICE set out to reinvent a global icon.” (2021-12-06). Exit framed as "a new chapter," with a board seat — no reason given.

Amanda Hindlian (FIDS President 2022–23)

From NYSE capital markets; hosted the 2022 Fixed Income Forum. Twenty items, mostly product quotes: “The integration of data and technology within bond markets is helping re-shape the way firms execute trading strategies” (2022-10-25). Even index launches carry the script: “connecting customers and investors to opportunity” (2022-01-19). Left after 22 months rather than move to Atlanta.

Tim Bowler — IBA President (to 2022) → clearing role → IMT President (by Mar 2023 – late 2025)

The LIBOR-transition voice of 2019–22 (about 20 IBA releases) became the face of the FTC fight: “We are disappointed that the FTC has filed litigation to prevent ICE from closing our acquisition of Black Knight” (2023-03-09). On the podcast: “We could have never done that without making the acquisition of Black Knight.” Origination “it's as low as it's been since the early 1990s”; the parent pays: “none of the businesses on an individual basis, if they were standalone, would have anything near the capital budget that we have today”; mission: “Breaking down legacy guild mentalities”; forecasting: “it's never a good idea to predict anything in the financial markets” (all 2024-11-04). Shift: the career move mirrors ICE's — from benchmark run-off to mortgage workflow.

Joe Tyrrell (IMT President 2020–22) and Bob Hart (2026–)

Tyrrell, the Ellie Mae inheritance, is the most practitioner-sounding leader: “the only thing worse than a bad process is an automated bad process.” “This isn't a technology issue. This is more of a design issue. It's a tradition issue.” Tyrrell adopts the house line fast — “at ICE we've always been a FinTech” — and names the competitive model: “Our business model actually incorporates that co-opetition into it.” (all 2022-03-21). Not quoted after 2022-03-31. Hart (from Feb 2026) speaks product-AI: “responsible automation- and AI-driven productivity agents” (2026-03-17); “Fraud reviews are often fragmented and highly manual” (2026-06-01).

Peter Borstelmann & Marshall Nicholson (ICE Bonds)

Nicholson launched ICE Bonds and ICE Select: “our customers need sophisticated trading tools that provide access to liquidity across fixed income markets” (2020-04-29). Borstelmann (31 items) is the volume-record voice — growth “primarily driven by increased adoption of our trading protocols by a combination of retail-oriented brokerage firms and institutional investors” (2025-02-18) — and announced the MarketAxess link: “This collaboration connects two mature liquidity networks in fixed income markets to offer new trading and risk management solutions for clients” (2024-08-05). The release names Borstelmann "Pete."

Elizabeth King — CRO → ESG → all clearinghouses (2024–)

Ex-SEC, KCG, NYSE GC. 2022–23 King is ICE's climate voice (about ten ESG releases; last: “Capital markets will continue to play a critical role in financing decarbonization and the energy transition,” 2023-09-20). From Jan 2024 King runs six clearinghouses and the ESG team moves to Edmonds. No attributed quote after the move. Inference: the ESG retreat (§3) shows up as a person going quiet.

Trabue Bland, Jeff Barbuto, Gordon Bennett — the futures franchise

Bland (23 items) narrates records and new asset classes: “ICE’s purpose is to create markets to allow our customers to manage their risk” (2023-01-27, EU gas cap); compute “is in desperate need of a globally accepted pricing mechanism and risk management tool” (2026-05-19). Barbuto (36 items) runs the anti-Cushing campaign: “the traditional WTI Cushing benchmark has lost relevance, with pricing power shifting to Houston where U.S. crude meets global markets” (2025-07-18). Bennett (44 items, the most prolific product voice) is frank on carbon: “If you become sort of a net zero zealot”; avoided-emission credits mean “you're effectively still getting paid to pollute.” (2022-06-01) — then by 2026 the line is tenure: “Steadily over 25 years, ICE has built the largest and most liquid energy and environmental markets in the world” (2026-01-30).

Michael Blaugrund & Jon Herrick — the tokenization pair

Blaugrund (NYSE COO from 2019; "prior roles with Nasdaq, Thomson Reuters and Tradeweb," 2019-06-03) is by 2026 ICE's VP of Strategic Initiatives. Script: “Since its founding, ICE has propelled markets from analog to digital” (2026-01-19); “We moved from manual to electronic, we're now moving from electronic to digital.” Regulatory claim: “we don't require any meaningful regulatory exemptions. We don't require any legislative action.” Herrick: “there's a comfort with what it means to operate clearinghouses to custody assets that is inherent in the DNA of ICE.” (all 2026-02-18).

Mark Wassersug — COO → CIO (exit 2023)

The operator's memoir: “I've been involved in 33 acquisitions and integrations in my time at ICE.” Origins: “We were a ragtag bunch of guys from Atlanta who had no street cred”. Admits cloud lag: “We are only beginning to dip our toe into that area.” And the public plea to the founder: “Jeff, please give the ops people some time to do the integration” (all 2023-01-03) — six months before Black Knight closed.

Clearing: Paul Hamill, Stan Ivanov, Hester Serafini

Hamill is the challenger-CCP pitchman: “Our goal is to make 2026 a year of competition and choice for market participants.” (2025-09-03). Ivanov (14 items) is the membership-and-milestones voice of ICE Clear Credit. Serafini (PhD mathematician, ex-Goldman/JPM) was picked after “reviewing an extensive list of internal and external candidates” (Edmonds, 2020-06-18) and runs risk-model change: “By assessing risk on a portfolio basis, IRM 2 is able to calculate risk precisely” (2025-11-17).

Clive de Ruig (IBA), Varun Pawar (Data CPO), Andy Walden / Julian Grey (mortgage data)

de Ruig's voice is regulatory: “IBA is pleased to have been granted recognition by ESMA” (2026-02-10). Pawar launches the AI products (ICE Compass: “Finding useful, pre-trade intelligence in the enormous amount of data that buyside firms are bombarded with each day has become increasingly difficult,” 2026-06-09) and interviews colleagues with the founder's framing: “at multiple town halls, multiple investor calls, Jeff, our CEO, speaks about ICE as an all-weather company” (2025-05-12). Both data voices came with Black Knight: Walden, “the synergies are phenomenal” but “I'm not here to sell Lance a bill of goods” (2024-01-16); Grey (the host says "Her leadership"), “we're helping our clients build all-weather businesses” and “In some ways data and analytics failed the industry back in 2007.” (2025-05-12).

Sharon Bowen and the board

Bowen (ICE director since 2017, ex-CFTC commissioner, NYSE Chair from 2022) explains why a regulator joined: “ICE in particular was extremely well managed, very proactive in terms of regulation.” “A founder led company creates a different culture.” Director rule: “Your job is not to run the company.” (all 2022-02-14). The 2022 refresh removed the three directors who had served “since before we went public in 2005” (Sprecher, 2022-03-04). Lord Hill (ex-EU financial-services commissioner, HM Treasury lead NED) joined in 2025, praising “a resilient, all-weather, entrepreneurial-focused company” — the outside director already speaking the script.

Josh King — head of communications and host (to Aug 2024)

The candour channel. On Bakkt futures: “We thought there'd be a market, there wasn't.” (2023-08-14). On CME's market cap: “You don't think we check that score just about every day?” (2023-03-09). On the Atlanta founder: “In some ways, he's a distant chair of the NYSE” (2022-02-14). Read: ICE lets its own host say what releases never do; after King, the podcast turns to product episodes.

4. Communication style and narrative craft

Sprecher — the folksy contrarian. Short declaratives ("I've never been the low bidder"), self-deprecation (least qualified NYSE chair, rejected by the All-In Summit while Sprecher's spouse was accepted — Sprecher's own anecdote), and parables (Geithner's barn, Enron "may have stolen the idea," the $1 or $1,000 purchase). Sprecher refuses forward guidance on air. Contrast with Tradeweb's Hult: Hult narrates an era; Sprecher narrates a pattern.

The house script, with first sightings and diffusion: - analog to digital — 2019 letter ("moving analog to digital"); Ellie Mae release headline (2020-08-06); 2020–2024 letters; Tyrrell (6× in one 2022 episode), Edmonds (2022, 2024), Blaugrund (2026). Edmonds attributes it: "You've heard our CEO." - all-weather — first in the Dec 2021 staff letter ("an all-weather performer"); 2022 letter 5×; every earnings release from 2Q22; Gardiner (2022), Bowler, Grey, Pawar, Lord Hill. Pawar's line makes the source explicit: town halls and investor calls. - connect people to opportunity — 2021 letter ("The heart of our ICE strategy"); ad tagline in every 2022–24 podcast; Hindlian (2022), Edmonds (2023); the 2022 letter uses it as all four section headings. - neutral / Switzerland — Sprecher 2019; letter 2025. - integration / imprint — Jackson 2018; Tuttle: “you can't have two cultures when you're bringing companies together.” (2022-11-07).

Product heads speak in records and tenure. Bland, Barbuto, Bennett and Borstelmann announce "record" days and "over two decades" of building; almost none of the 30+ quoted executives gives a forward number.

What they never talk about: a successor; executive pay; why Cunningham, Hindlian, Tyrrell or Bowler moved on; Bakkt after 2023; the FTC's reasoning; MarketAxess as a competitor before 2024; the PennyMac fight beyond one release; layoffs; the return-to-office fight (King mentions "four days a week," 2024-08-12, once).

5. Culture and talent, as the leaders describe it

  • Founder origin as identity. Two founders calling on 106–108 firms; "ragtag" Atlanta engineers; day-one prices "inverted" (Wassersug). Sprecher on the people bond: “It was like being in the military together” (2024-08-12).
  • Imprint, flatten, debate. Jackson's integration creed (healthy debate, open door, no fiefdoms) plus Sprecher's productive-conflict class; Edmonds quotes the founder: “I'm okay if we fail, I'm not okay making the same mistake twice.” (2022-06-27).
  • Generalists over specialists. The rotation table above is the talent model: a broker runs data, a benchmark lawyer-regulator type runs mortgage, a GC runs clearing. Bowen's word for the result is "founder led"; inference: the CEO's judgment of people substitutes for a formal pipeline.
  • Regulator fluency as a hiring criterion. Bowen, Klima, King (ex-SEC), Lord Hill, Bryan Daniel (Texas state government). ICE recruits people who have sat on the other side of the table.
  • Office and place. ICE is at four days a week (King, 2024); FIDS leadership must sit in Atlanta (2023–24).
  • Absent: headcount trend beyond "nearly 10,000" (2021) and "around 16,000" with Black Knight (host King, 2022-06-27); attrition; equity culture; how Black Knight people were retained beyond the two data voices on air.

6. Leadership lenses

  • canon schein organizational culture — Artifacts: the podcast, the ad tagline, the Atlanta HQ, the NYSE floor. Espoused values: neutrality, transparency, "all-weather." Basic assumption: the founder's pattern-recognition is the strategy; leaders are interchangeable carriers of it. That assumption explains why roles rotate and the script repeats.
  • canon jensen meckling agency theory — a 26-year founder-CEO-Chair with a board refreshed by that CEO (three founding-era directors out in 2022; new directors from subsidiary boards) concentrates control; the eBay retreat (2020) shows shareholders are the binding check, not the board (ice outside voices).
  • canon pfeffer power — power sits with Sprecher and Jackson (deal + integration); segment heads are powerful only while they hold the seat. Location (Atlanta) is a power resource.
  • canon kotter leading change — contrast with Tradeweb's ten-month guided handover; ICE has no guiding coalition for succession, only for each deal (integration team owns the deal).
  • canon grove high output management — Wassersug's standardization (“scale exponentially without having to scale our staff exponentially”, 2023-01-03) is Grove's leverage argument; the plea to pause deals is the managerial-capacity constraint made public.
  • canon horowitz what you do is who you are — the diversity test: the board went to six of ten seats held by women while the CEO disavowed "box ticking." What ICE did is the board; what it says shifted.
  • canon tetlock superforecasting — Bowler's "never a good idea to predict" and Sprecher's no-guidance stance versus a mortgage segment "spring-loaded" for falling rates: the forecast is embedded in capital allocation, not in words.

7. ICE vs Tradeweb: two people systems (see tradeweb people)

Dimension ICE Tradeweb
Top tenure Sprecher founder-CEO 26 yrs, no named successor Olesky CEO 2008–22 → Hult, announced 10 months ahead
No. 2 Jackson President throughout President role tried (Pluta, 21 months) then abolished
CFO IR head promoted (Gardiner) Outside hire (Furber, ex-IEX); IR head (Serrao) never quoted
Development Cross-segment rotation (clearing → data; benchmarks → mortgage) Long tenure inside one product line (Bruni, Bruner, Conlin)
Board feeder Subsidiary boards (Ellie Mae, IMT/MERS, Endex, ICE Clear Europe) Board → management (Pluta, Dixon); LSEG seats
House script "analog to digital," "all-weather," "connect people to opportunity" "collaborative innovation," "secret sauce," "one-size-fits-all" (as what TW isn't)
Candour outlet Host Josh King; Edmonds on air Bruner's "these are estimates"; Dixon's TRACE blog
Shared person Michael Blaugrund — ex-Tradeweb, NYSE COO 2019, ICE tokenization lead 2026 Same; the corpus shows no Tradeweb comment

Read: Tradeweb's continuity is in people (insiders in one seat for decades); ICE's is in the founder and the script (people move, the words stay). Both promote from within; Tradeweb hires outsiders for missing functions, ICE hires outsiders for regulatory credibility.

Rep

Part A (E4, board math). Using §1: compute the share of women on the ICE board at each point — Dec 2020 (14 seats, 5 women), May 2022 (10 seats, 6 women), Sep 2025 (11 seats, assume Lord Hill is the only change). Then state what a governance analyst should make of a board that shrank by four seats in 17 months while the CEO also chairs it. Answer: 5/14 = 35.7%; 6/10 = 60%; 6/11 = 54.5%. A smaller board refreshed by a founder-chair is more diverse and more cohesive but less independent of management; the counterweight is a Lead Independent Director (Noonan from 2022) and, in practice, shareholders (eBay, 2020).

Part B (E1, succession memo, ≤300 words). You are ICE's Lead Independent Director. Rank three internal candidates — Jackson, Edmonds, Martin — on (1) breadth of segments run, (2) regulatory fluency, (3) deal/integration record, (4) public voice. Cite one line from §2 per candidate. Model scoring: Jackson 3 segments-by-oversight, deals and integration, low public voice; Edmonds clearing + data + marketing, mandate fluency, "refereeing… the performance"; Martin data + NYSE, politics and listings, the most quoted (63 items). The memo should note no candidate has run mortgage, the segment with ~$25B of capital in it.

Part C (E7). Rewrite Bowler's "none of the businesses on an individual basis…" line as a 40-word investor answer that a CFO trained in IR (Gardiner) would give, using "all-weather" once and a number from the note (origination at early-1990s lows).
